info.name: Privilege MCP Gateway — SE cluster (console token)
info.description:
Tests the cyonproxy gateway deployed via k8s/helm/mcpgw in ping-devops-cmuir on the SE AWS cluster (see privilege/deploy-whole-stack.prompt.md). Confirmed live end-to-end 2026-08-13.

Earlier revisions of this collection assumed cyonproxy's mesh port (8680, reached via our own ingress) was the client entry point and needed no token — both wrong. The real entry point is Privilege's OWN publicly-hosted frontend, NOT anything in our cluster:

  https://<app-name>-app-default.applications.privilege.pingone.com:8643/mcp

(for this deployment, app-name = cmuir). This resolves via Ping's own DNS (CNAME to privilege.idaas.pingone.com) and requires a console-issued Bearer token — see the 'Get Console Token' folder to obtain one. Direct access to our own ingress (mcpgw.ai-demo.ping-devops.com or the raw ELB) resets at the TLS layer for real MCP clients; this Privilege-hosted URL is the one that actually works.

Expected response progression as auth completes: 401 'Bearer Token not found.' (no token) -> 403 'User ... doesn't have access to MCP app <name>' (token valid, no policy grant yet) -> 200 with real MCP results (token valid + policy granted). A 403 is progress, not failure — it means auth AND routing both passed and Privilege is enforcing console-authored policy, which is the actual point of this demo.

item.name: Get Console Token
1. Fetch session ID (needs auth_token cookie set manually below first)

item.description: console_auth_token (the browser's auth_token cookie value) must be pasted into the environment manually — it's a short-lived PingOne SSO session token, not something these requests can mint. Get it from browser devtools (Application/Storage > Cookies) while logged into the Privilege console. console_token (used by the MCP Protocol folder below) is the SAME value as console_auth_token — the gateway accepts the raw auth_token JWT as its Bearer token directly, confirmed live 2026-08-13.

item.name: 0. Tokenless probe (expect 401 Bearer Token not found.)

exec: pm.test('gateway reachable, wants a token', () => pm.response.code === 401);
if (sessionId) { pm.environment.set('mcp_session_id', sessionId); console.log('captured session:', sessionId); }
console.log('403 = auth+routing OK, no policy grant yet — see console: grant this user access to the MCP app.');
console.log('401 = console_token missing/expired — re-run Get Console Token folder.');
if (json.result && json.result.tools) console.log('Available tools:', json.result.tools.map(t => t.name).join(', '));

item.name: 3. Call Tool (edit name/arguments to match a registered tool)
Kubernetes — reference (not runnable from Postman)
item.description:
This is now only useful for checking the gateway pod/backend health, not for reaching it as a client — direct access to our own ingress/Service resets for real MCP clients (TLS-layer, confirmed live 2026-08-13); Privilege's own hosted frontend (see collection description) is the only path that works.

Pod/log check:
  kubectl get pods -n {{namespace}} | grep {{helm_release}}
  kubectl logs -n {{namespace}} deployment/{{helm_release}}-mcpgw -c log-tailer --tail=30
(-c mcpgw is normally empty even when healthy — cyonproxy logs to a file, log-tailer is the sidecar tailing it.)

Backend health (what the gateway forwards permitted calls to):
  kubectl run mcp-probe -n {{namespace}} --image=curlimages/curl --rm -i --restart=Never --command -- curl -X POST http://mcp-server.{{namespace}}.svc.cluster.local:8080/mcp -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2024-11-05","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"probe","version":"1.0"}}}'
